lesson.title: First Impressions That Stick: The Primacy Effect
lesson.summary: The primacy effect is the tendency to remember the earliest items in a sequence better than those that follow, largely because they receive more rehearsal and a better chance at long-term storage.
lesson.body:
The primacy effect is the half of the serial position effect that explains why items near the beginning of a list tend to be remembered unusually well. It is not simply that people pay more attention at the start out of curiosity, though that may play a small role; the more important reason has to do with how rehearsal and long-term storage actually work.

When a list first begins, there is little else competing for a learner's attention, so the first few items receive a disproportionate share of available rehearsal. As each new item arrives, a person can silently repeat not just the newest item but the earlier ones as well, since working memory is not yet full. By the time several more items have appeared, however, attention has to be divided across a growing set of things to hold in mind, and each individual item, including the early ones already committed to memory, gets comparatively less rehearsal per item than the first ones did. Under the logic of the multi-store model, more rehearsal early on translates into a better chance of transferring those early items from short-term into durable long-term storage. This is also what makes the primacy effect resistant to delay: because early items have often already been consolidated into long-term memory, they are still recoverable even after a distraction or a delay between study and test, unlike recency items, which depend on immediate access to short-term memory and fade quickly once something else occupies attention.

Imagine a student memorizing a list of twenty vocabulary words presented one at a time, a few seconds apart. By the time the fifth word appears, she has already silently repeated the first word several times over. By the time the fifteenth word appears, her attention is split so many ways that no single word, old or new, gets much individual rehearsal. If she is tested immediately after seeing the full list, she will likely recall both the first few words and the last few words well. But if the test is delayed by a day, something changes: the last few words, which she remembered mainly because they were still sitting in short-term memory moments earlier, are now largely gone, while the first few words, which received real rehearsal and had time to consolidate, are still there.

The primacy effect is best understood as one half of the broader serial position effect, paired with its counterpart, the recency effect, and it foreshadows a theme that becomes explicit in the discussion of maintenance and elaborative rehearsal: not all rehearsal is created equal, but repeated exposure of any kind, given early and often enough, meaningfully increases the odds that information makes the trip into long-term memory.

This is also why teachers and presenters often put their most important point first: whatever arrives when a listener's attention and rehearsal capacity are least divided has a genuine, well-documented edge at surviving into long-term memory.
